AgentSentry: Mitigating Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents via Temporal Causal Diagnostics and Context PurificationThanks: 6 Corresponding author.

PubID: pubid: Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium 2027 22–26 March 2027, Seoul, Republic of Korea ISBN 978-1-970672-09-1 https://dx.doi.org/10.14722/ndss.2027.230441 www.ndss-symposium.org
Tian Zhang2, Yiwei Xu2, Juan Wang26, Keyan Guo4, Xiaoyang Xu2, Bowen Xiao2, Quanlong Guan3,
Jinlin Fan2, Jiawei Liu2, Zhiquan Liu3, Hongxin Hu4 Affiliation: 2School of Cyber Science and Engineering, Wuhan University, 4University at Buffalo, 3Jinan University
Email: 2{tianzhang2025, yiweix, jwang, xiaoyangx, bwxiao, mmdx_t}@whu.edu.cn, ljw2804@stu.ouc.edu.cn
4{keyanguo, hongxinh}@buffalo.edu, 3gql@jnu.edu.cn, zqliu@vip.qq.com
Abstract

Tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents aggregate dialogue history, tool outputs, and retrieved content into an accumulated runtime state to complete multi-step tasks. This execution model exposes agents to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, in which attacker-controlled instructions embedded in external artifacts enter the agent state and later influence tool use. Multi-turn IPI is especially challenging because injected content can persist across intermediate steps and trigger unauthorized state-changing actions only after it has been merged with user intent in the same context. This creates a source-attribution problem: existing inference-time defenses can often detect suspicious behavior but do not directly distinguish whether a pending action is supported by the user task or influenced by injected content. Consequently, they resort to conservative blocking, termination, or broad filtering, sacrificing utility for security. We propose AgentSentry, an inference-time defense that operationalizes temporal causal diagnostics through boundary-local counterfactual re-executions at tool-return boundaries. It substitutes the mediator under a restored snapshot, records whether the pending proposal survives, and aggregates user-view and probe scores across adjacent boundaries. When a proposal is mediator-sensitive, AgentSentry purifies the implicated mediator content while preserving task-relevant evidence and resumes execution from the sanitized state. We evaluate AgentSentry on AgentDojo across four task suites, three IPI attack families, and three black-box LLM backbones. AgentSentry records no observed successful attack in the evaluated cases (ASR=0%\mathrm{ASR}=0\%) and achieves an average Utility Under Attack (UA) of 76.10%76.10\%. Compared with the strongest evaluated baseline, AgentSentry improves average UA by 1.841.84–7.607.60 percentage points, with benign FPRs of 2.06%2.06\%–5.15%5.15\%. Additional evaluations examine long-horizon and adaptive attacks, imperfect purification, runtime overhead, and an OpenClaw engineering case study.

I Introduction

Tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute multi-step tasks by combining model outputs with external tools, retrieval systems, and enterprise services [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. During execution, the agent runtime accumulates dialogue history, intermediate tool outputs, retrieved passages, and memory into the context that guides subsequent planning and tool invocation [6, 7, 8]. This architecture enables long-horizon task completion, but it also expands the agent’s trust boundary by allowing external tool- or retrieval-returned content to enter the same context that later conditions model-generated actions.

Indirect prompt injection (IPI) exploits this tool-mediated context channel. Rather than controlling the user prompt, an attacker embeds instructions in external artifacts such as emails, documents, webpages, calendar entries, or retrieved records. When the agent later accesses these artifacts through legitimate tools or retrieval modules, attacker-written content can be incorporated into the execution context and treated as task-relevant evidence [9, 10, 11, 12]. A particularly difficult case is multi-turn IPI: the injected content may enter through an early read operation, persist across subsequent context updates, and only later influence a state-changing action at a write-capable boundary. Figure 1 illustrates the multi-turn tool-mediated IPI path, where attacker-controlled content enters through an early tool read and can influence a later pending action after being accumulated into the agent context.

This threat is relevant to practical deployments. Recent incidents and case studies indicate that artifact-mediated or tool-mediated prompt injection can affect systems that process external content through legitimate APIs, including a Microsoft 365 Copilot zero-click issue and code-interpreter-style data-exfiltration scenarios [13, 14, 15]. In many deployments, the application runtime can observe prompts, tool calls, tool returns, and pending actions, while the LLM backend remains a remote black box. This setting makes application-layer inference-time defense a practical deployment point when model retraining, provider-side instrumentation, or access to internal model states is unavailable [10, 16, 17].

Existing inference-time defenses remain limited because they do not directly resolve the source of control behind a pending action. Detection- and blocking-oriented defenses, such as trajectory re-execution and task-alignment guards, can flag suspicious behavior or prevent unsafe tool use, but typically respond by stopping execution or suppressing actions [16, 17]. Sanitization- and localization-based defenses reduce exposure to suspicious content, but they do not by themselves determine whether a risky pending proposal is mediator-sensitive under controlled substitution, nor do they re-derive a supported continuation once such sensitivity has been identified [18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. The resulting security–utility tension is not merely an efficiency issue: strong protection is often obtained by terminating, rolling back, or over-constraining otherwise benign multi-step workflows.

Our key observation is that multi-turn IPI creates a source-attribution problem at action time. After external content has been incorporated into the agent state, the same pending action may admit competing explanations. For example, sending an email may be a legitimate continuation of the user’s request, or it may depend on an instruction embedded in a retrieved document. Purely observational methods, such as lexical detectors, action-level alignment checks, and trajectory-level similarity tests, can flag suspicious behavior, but they do not directly establish which source the pending action depends on. This makes the core security question interventional at the runtime boundary: would the same pending action still be proposed if the implicated mediator content were locally purified while the user view and the remaining boundary state were held fixed?

To address these challenges, we propose AgentSentry, an inference-time defense framework for tool-augmented LLM agents. AgentSentry adopts an execution-level temporal attribution takeover abstraction: attacker influence need not manifest as an immediate abnormal action, but may persist through tool- and retrieval-mediated state updates and later make a consequential proposal sensitive to mediator content at a write-capable boundary.

AgentSentry operationalizes this idea through a diagnose-and-continue pipeline. At each tool-return boundary, it restores the boundary snapshot and performs side-effect-free counterfactual re-executions that substitute the user view and/or mediator content while holding the restored state, tool set, and decoding configuration fixed. The user-preserving mediator-purification contrast serves as the primary live-policy signal, the probe-conditional contrast provides corroborating evidence, and the user-view and probe trends are aggregated over a short window of adjacent boundaries so that a progressive shift toward mediator-supported behavior need not be decisive at any single one. When these signals identify a pending proposal as mediator-sensitive, AgentSentry purifies the implicated content, removing instruction-bearing control signals while preserving task-relevant evidence, then revises the pending action under the sanitized state and permits only authorized, evidence-supported effects, so the agent continues the original workflow rather than terminating execution or broadly suppressing tool use.

We evaluate AgentSentry on the AgentDojo benchmark [10] across four task suites, three IPI attack families, and three black-box LLM backbones, where it records zero observed successful attacks (ASR=0%\mathrm{ASR}=0\%) and an average Utility Under Attack (UA) of 76.10%76.10\%. Against the strongest evaluated baseline on each backbone, this improves average UA by 1.841.84–7.607.60 percentage points and reduces a residual average ASR of 1.54%1.54\%–7.26%7.26\% to zero observed successes, with benign FPRs of 2.06%2.06\%–5.15%5.15\%. Additional evaluations examine long-horizon and adaptive attacks, imperfect purification, threshold sensitivity, representative failures, and attacked- and benign-path overhead, together with an OpenClaw engineering case study [23, 24]. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We formalize multi-turn IPI as a source-attribution problem in multi-turn agent execution, where trusted user-goal signals and untrusted tool-, retrieval-, or memory-mediated content are merged into an accumulating state before later actions are proposed.

  • •

    We propose AgentSentry, an inference-time defense that adopts an execution-level temporal attribution takeover abstraction and realizes an integrated diagnose-and-continue pipeline at tool-return boundaries.

  • •

    We design a boundary-local controlled re-execution protocol that summarizes controlled runtime contrasts as replay-based attribution scores and couples them with targeted context purification, action revision, and effect gating for safe continuation.

  • •

    We evaluate AgentSentry on AgentDojo across multiple task suites, IPI attack families, and black-box LLM backbones, together with long-horizon, adaptive-attack, purification- robustness, and overhead analyses, and further conduct an OpenClaw engineering case study in a deployed-style local-agent setting.11 1 Our code is available at https://github.com/CyberGuardianAI/AgentSentry.

II Related Work

II-A Tool-Augmented LLM Agents and Indirect Prompt Injection

Modern LLM agents increasingly interact with external tools, retrieval systems, and mutable environments to complete real-world tasks. Early agent frameworks relied on manually specified tool interfaces [3, 2], while later work showed that tool-use behavior can also be acquired from demonstrations or synthetic supervision [1, 25, 8, 26]. Commercial systems further expose unified multi-tool and multi-modal capabilities [27].

This tool-augmented setting also introduces a distinct attack surface. When agents ingest heterogeneous and partially untrusted artifacts such as emails, documents, or web pages, adversarial instructions embedded in these artifacts may be incorporated into the evolving context and subsequently affect downstream planning and tool use. This threat is commonly referred to as indirect prompt injection (IPI) [9]. Benchmarks such as InjecAgent [28] and AgentDojo [10] formalize this setting in multi-step, multi-tool environments, showing that injected external content can trigger unsafe behavior under benign user requests.

II-B IPI Attacks

Existing IPI attacks broadly fall into two categories. The first targets general weaknesses in instruction following and prompt boundary separation. Representative examples include reusable injection templates, control-token patterns, and explicit instruction overrides that cause the model to ignore prior context or safety constraints [29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35].

The second category exploits the structure of specific agent environments. Web agents are vulnerable to environmental and context-based injections that manipulate perception and action routines [36, 37, 28]. Computer-use agents can be affected by adversarial interface patterns [38], while multimodal agents can be influenced by visually embedded prompts [39]. These attacks do not require control of the user prompt; instead, they operate through external content channels that the agent later treats as task-relevant context [40].

II-C Inference-Time Defenses

Defenses against prompt injection can be broadly grouped into training-time and inference-time approaches. Training-time methods improve robustness through adversarial fine-tuning or related optimization procedures [41, 42, 43], or train dedicated detectors for suspicious inputs and traces [44]. While effective in some settings, these methods often require model access and substantial retraining costs, limiting their applicability to deployed black-box agents.

Inference-time defenses instead operate at runtime. Prompt-level methods separate or annotate untrusted content using delimiters, authentication tags, or known-answer detection prompts [45, 46, 31]. Tool-policy defenses constrain tool use through allowlists or task-specific control policies [10, 47]. IPIGuard [48] extends this line of defense by constructing a tool-dependency graph to constrain injection-induced tool-use paths. Sanitization and localization defenses, including PromptArmor [18], DataFilter [19], Soft Instruction De-escalation Defense [20], CommandSans [21], and PromptLocate [22], suppress, rewrite, or localize instruction-bearing content before it influences downstream behavior.

Agent-level and runtime-trace guards provide another runtime defense family. MELON [16] uses masked re-execution to detect trajectory inconsistencies, while Task Shield [17] checks whether proposed actions align with the user objective. AgentSentinel [7] targets computer-use agents by intercepting sensitive operations and auditing execution traces. AgentArmor [49] applies program analysis to agent runtime traces to enforce execution-time constraints against prompt injection, while TraceAegis [50] combines hierarchical trace analysis with behavioral anomaly detection. These systems provide useful runtime protection signals through action checking, trace analysis, and anomaly detection, but commonly respond by rejecting, constraining, or terminating suspicious execution paths. In multi-turn IPI, this can prevent attacks but may also truncate benign workflows once ambiguity arises.

II-D Attribution- and Provenance-Based Defenses

Within the broader family of inference-time defenses, recent work has begun to use attribution and provenance signals to identify which context source influences agent behavior. CausalArmor [51] uses causal ablation to estimate the influence of untrusted context segments and sanitizes segments that exert disproportionate control over agent behavior. AttriGuard [52] performs action-level attribution for each proposed tool invocation independently, re-executing the agent under a control-attenuated view of external observations. ProvSEEK [53] uses LLM-driven provenance forensics to support threat investigation and detection.

Unlike these approaches, AgentSentry holds the observed user view fixed and substitutes only the mediator, so the resulting contrast is referenced to the pending proposal itself rather than to an ablated context segment or to a probe-induced action. It additionally tracks the user-view and probe-conditional scores across a short window and reuses the same projection as the repair applied to the live state, allowing the original workflow to continue under a repaired boundary state. Our focus is therefore boundary-level attribution with safe continuation, rather than segment-level sanitization, action-level attribution, or provenance-oriented forensic analysis alone.

III Problem Setting

III-A Agent Model and Execution Semantics

We formalize a tool-augmented LLM agent as a composable state transformer operating over an internal task context and an external environment. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} denote the internal state space representing the agent context, including the dialogue history, intermediate reasoning artifacts, tool outputs, retrieval snippets, and persistent memory. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} denote the action space, where an action may contain a natural-language response and a (possibly empty) sequence of tool calls with arguments. Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} denote the external environment state space (e.g., inbox, calendar, file system, and third-party services) that can be queried and modified by tool executions.

Context-to-action policy. The LLM is modeled as a context-to-action transformer

TLLM:𝒞→𝒜,T_{\mathrm{LLM}}:\ \mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}, (1)

which maps a context c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} to a proposed next action a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}.

Runtime context update and external effects. The agent runtime is modeled by two transformers that update the internal context and commit side effects to the external environment:

Tint:𝒜×𝒞→𝒞,Text:𝒜×𝒪→𝒪.T_{\mathrm{int}}:\ \mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{C},\qquad T_{\mathrm{ext}}:\ \mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}. (2)

Here TintT_{\mathrm{int}} appends tool returns and retrieved content into the task context, and TextT_{\mathrm{ext}} applies the corresponding external effects. One iteration of the agent loop is

T⁡(c,o)=(Tint​(a,c),Text​(a,o)),where ​a=TLLM​(c).T(c,o)=\bigl(T_{\mathrm{int}}(a,c),\ T_{\mathrm{ext}}(a,o)\bigr),\quad\text{where }a=T_{\mathrm{LLM}}(c). (3)

III-B Deployment Setting and Threat Model

We consider a tool-augmented LLM agent whose application runtime executes locally while next-step generation is obtained from a remote black-box LLM API. The runtime maintains the dialogue state, serializes model inputs, dispatches tool and retrieval calls, stores intermediate results, and commits externally visible side effects. As illustrated in Figure 1, our goal is to defend this application-layer pipeline against IPI under this black-box setting.

Trust boundary. We trust the local runtime, including the system prompt, tool wrappers, authorization logic, deployment policy, and the snapshot-and-restore mechanism used by the defense. We do not trust externally sourced content once it enters the workflow, even when returned through legitimate tools; emails, webpages, retrieved passages, shared documents, database records, and persistent notes originating outside the runtime are all treated as untrusted. The remote LLM is likewise a black box: the defender may query it, but cannot inspect or modify model parameters, hidden states, or provider-side safeguards.

Attacker capability. The attacker cannot control the user request, the local runtime, the system prompt, the tool schema, or the model provider, but can inject malicious text into external content channels the agent may later access, for instance by sending an email, publishing a webpage, editing a shared document or calendar entry, inserting a database record, or poisoning a persistent note. The attack proceeds indirectly: attacker-authored content is returned through normal tool use, retrieval, or memory recall, serialized into the agent context, and may influence later reasoning and action selection.

Attack goal and success criterion. The attacker aims to induce an unauthorized high-impact action that violates user intent or deployment policy, such as exfiltrating private data, sending an unauthorized message, or performing a destructive state change. An attack succeeds only if such an action is committed to the external environment. We additionally record whether the undefended agent proposes such an action, since without an application-layer safeguard the runtime would normally execute it.

Defender scope. The defender operates at the application layer and controls the local runtime. It may cache and restore tool-return boundaries, reuse recorded tool or retrieval returns, perform side-effect-free re-executions, substitute a sanitized mediator view, revise a pending action, and withhold an unresolved external effect. The defender does not require model parameters, hidden states, gradients, fine-tuning, or provider-side modifications.

Out of scope. We exclude direct malicious user prompts, compromised local runtimes or tool executors, malicious tool schemas, operating-system or network compromise, and collusion by the model provider.

III-C Source-Attribution Problem

The threat model above induces a boundary-local source-attribution problem. At a tool-return boundary bb, newly returned tool, retrieval, or memory content has entered the agent context before the next action is committed. We write the model-visible boundary context as

cb=hb⊕xb⊕rb,c_{b}=h_{b}\oplus x_{b}\oplus r_{b}, (4)

where hbh_{b} denotes the restored non-target runtime state held fixed across controlled re-execution regimes, xbx_{b} is the runtime-addressable user view, rbr_{b} is the runtime-addressable mediator view, and ⊕\oplus denotes runtime serialization. The replayable boundary snapshot is sb=(hb,xb,rb)s_{b}=(h_{b},x_{b},r_{b}).

Given sbs_{b}, a pending action aba_{b}, the trusted user goal gg, and deployment policy Π\Pi, the defender must determine whether the pending behavior remains supported by the user task or is sensitive to mediator content. The same action may be a legitimate continuation of the user request or may have been induced by an external artifact, so content screening alone is insufficient.

IV Design of AgentSentry

AgentSentry is an inference-time defense for tool-augmented LLM agents. It operates on the live execution trajectory and intervenes at tool-return boundaries, after mediator content has entered the local context and before the next action is committed. Figure 2 presents the pipeline. AgentSentry first performs boundary-local attribution diagnosis and then applies context purification and action revision to continue execution under a sanitized state.

IV-A Design Overview

AgentSentry implements the attribution problem in Section III-C as a two-stage runtime defense. All diagnostic executions are side-effect-free: replayed tool calls are not executed, and replayed external effects are never committed.

Stage 1: Boundary-local diagnosis. AgentSentry restores the boundary snapshot and evaluates the pending behavior under four controlled re-execution regimes. The regimes hold the restored non-target state fixed while varying the user-channel input and mediator view. Their outcomes are summarized by replay-based attribution scores. AgentSentry aggregates these contrasts over a short execution window to capture both abrupt and gradually emerging takeover.

Stage 2: Purified continuation. When takeover is detected, AgentSentry does not roll back the full trajectory or disable tool use. Instead, it purifies the implicated mediator content, revises the pending action under the repaired boundary state, and continues the original workflow when a supported continuation remains available. Externally visible effects are validated before commitment.

IV-B Stage 1: Boundary-Level Replay Model

We index pre-action decision points by tool-return boundaries ℬ={1,2,…}\mathcal{B}=\{1,2,\ldots\}. A boundary bb is the point immediately after newly obtained tool, retrieval, or memory content has entered the local context and immediately before the agent emits its next action. Let XbX_{b} denote the user-channel input, RbR_{b} the mediator view selected for replay, and AbA_{b} the next-action random variable induced by the base agent. Conditioned on the restored boundary snapshot, we write

Ab=fA​(Xb,hb,Rb,UbA),A_{b}=f_{A}(X_{b},h_{b},R_{b},U_{b}^{A}), (5)

where UbAU_{b}^{A} captures model-side variation, including decoding stochasticity. The pair (Xb,Rb)(X_{b},R_{b}) is the intervention target: each replay regime in Section IV-D fixes it to a declared value while holding hbh_{b}, the tool set, and the decoding configuration constant. Proposals obtained under different regimes are compared by their normalized action structure. For a proposal aa, let E⁡(a)E(a) denote the collection of parsed tool invocations it proposes and nl⁡(a)\mathrm{nl}(a) its natural-language component. For an invocation ee, write ϕ⁡(e)≜(tool⁡(e),ν⁡(args⁡(e)))\phi(e)\triangleq(\operatorname{tool}(e),\,\nu(\operatorname{args}(e))). The canonical structural signature is

σ(a)≜{{ϕ⁡(e):e∈E⁡(a)},E⁡(a)≠∅,{(𝚃𝙴𝚇𝚃,ν⁡(nl⁡(a)))},E(a)=∅,ν(nl(a))≠ε,{(𝙽𝙾𝙾𝙿,∅)},otherwise,\sigma(a)\triangleq\begin{cases}\{\phi(e):e\in E(a)\},&E(a)\neq\varnothing,\\[4.0pt] \{(\mathtt{TEXT},\nu(\mathrm{nl}(a)))\},&E(a)=\varnothing,\ \nu(\mathrm{nl}(a))\neq\varepsilon,\\[4.0pt] \{(\mathtt{NOOP},\varnothing)\},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (6)

where tool⁡(e)\operatorname{tool}(e) is the canonical endpoint name parsed from invocation ee, args⁡(e)\operatorname{args}(e) its complete argument map, ν⁡(⋅)\nu(\cdot) a type-aware canonicalization of structured arguments and text, and ε\varepsilon the empty string. Canonicalization covers the complete argument map rather than a subset of policy-sensitive keys, so two proposals invoking the same endpoint with any differing argument key or normalized value have distinct signatures; when a proposal contains tool invocations, its natural-language component does not enter the signature. For proposals aa and a′a^{\prime}, define the structural-matching predicate

m(a,a′)≜𝕀[σ(a)=σ(a′)].m(a,a^{\prime})\triangleq\mathbb{I}\!\left[\sigma(a)=\sigma(a^{\prime})\right]. (7)

The exact canonicalization rules are specified in Appendix A-A.

IV-C Stage 1: Boundary Instrumentation and Replay Operators

At each boundary bb, AgentSentry stores a replayable snapshot of the local runtime state, and the replay cache reuses the same tool, retrieval, or memory return across regimes without re-querying the external environment. All replay executions run in dry-run mode: the model may propose tool calls, but none is executed and no external effect is committed. Two operators act at the boundary, a masking operator on the user channel and a purification operator on the mediator channel.

Masking operator. Inside replay, the masking operator replaces the runtime-addressable user view xbx_{b} with a fixed masking probe xbmaskx_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}}, preserving the restored state, tool availability, mediator realization, and decoding configuration. The probe asks whether the visible tool, retrieval, or memory content attempts to govern the agent and, when applicable, returns complete verbatim control evidence together with a probe-induced candidate action. Ordinary procedures or factual parameter claims are not treated as control solely because they mention a possible action. Audit records produced under the probe serve dry-run diagnosis only and never enter the live trajectory.

Purification operator. Control-bearing spans reported in the audit records produced under the masking probe are aligned to the cached mediator and collected in a grounded evidence set 𝒢b\mathcal{G}_{b}. AgentSentry then constructs

rb(san)≜𝖯𝗎𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(rb,𝒢b).r_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})}\triangleq\mathsf{Purify}(r_{b};\mathcal{G}_{b}). (8)

The operator performs deterministic span alignment, range merging, and schema-preserving projection. Content outside the selected ranges is retained.

IV-D Stage 1: Four-Regime Counterfactual Replay

Given the observed user input xbx_{b}, the fixed masking probe xbmaskx_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}}, the cached mediator rbr_{b}, and the sanitized mediator rb(san)r_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})}, AgentSentry constructs four counterfactual replay regimes:

orig:\displaystyle\texttt{orig}: (Xb=xb,Rb=rb),\displaystyle(X_{b}=x_{b},\ R_{b}=r_{b}), (9)
mask:\displaystyle\texttt{mask}: (Xb=xbmask,Rb=rb),\displaystyle(X_{b}=x_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}},\ R_{b}=r_{b}),
mask_sanitized:\displaystyle\texttt{mask\_sanitized}: (Xb=xbmask,Rb=rb(san)),\displaystyle(X_{b}=x_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}},\ R_{b}=r_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})}),
orig_sanitized:\displaystyle\texttt{orig\_sanitized}: (Xb=xb,Rb=rb(san)).\displaystyle(X_{b}=x_{b},\ R_{b}=r_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})}).

The orig regime preserves the observed user view and mediator, and mask evaluates the same mediator under the fixed masking probe. Their sanitized counterparts, mask_sanitized and orig_sanitized, repeat each after purification. Operationally, orig and mask are executed first, followed by the sanitized regimes when the sanitized mediator is available; equivalent outcomes may be reused. A regime that cannot be constructed is marked unavailable, leaving the boundary inapplicable to the local gate under the zero-fill convention of Section IV-F.

For each available regime ι\iota and index k∈{1,…,Kb}k\in\{1,\ldots,K_{b}\}, where KbK_{b} is the effective replay count at boundary bb, the side-effect-free re-execution produces a candidate action ab(ι,k)a_{b}^{(\iota,k)}. We write aba_{b} for the representative proposal under orig, abmaska_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}} for the control-positive action parsed from mask, and ab(san)a_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})} for the proposal under orig_sanitized. If the probe yields no control-positive action, abmaska_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}} is not instantiated and SbM=0S_{b}^{M}=0. For a reference action aa, define its regime-wise structural survival rate as

p^bι​(a)≜1Kb​∑k=1Kbm⁡(ab(ι,k),a).\widehat{p}_{b}^{\iota}(a)\triangleq\frac{1}{K_{b}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{b}}m\!\left(a_{b}^{(\iota,k)},a\right). (10)

The replay budget and decoding configuration are specified in Appendix A-B.

IV-E Stage 1: Replay-Based Attribution Scores

At a fixed tool-return boundary bb, AgentSentry computes four replay-based attribution scores:

SbU\displaystyle S_{b}^{U} =p^borig​(ab)−p^bmask​(ab),\displaystyle=\widehat{p}_{b}^{\texttt{orig}}(a_{b})-\widehat{p}_{b}^{\texttt{mask}}(a_{b}), (11)
SbM\displaystyle S_{b}^{M} =p^bmask​(abmask)−p^bmask_sanitized​(abmask),\displaystyle=\widehat{p}_{b}^{\texttt{mask}}(a_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}})-\widehat{p}_{b}^{\texttt{mask\_sanitized}}(a_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}}), (12)
SbR\displaystyle S_{b}^{R} =p^borig_sanitized​(ab)−p^bmask_sanitized​(ab),\displaystyle=\widehat{p}_{b}^{\texttt{orig\_sanitized}}(a_{b})-\widehat{p}_{b}^{\texttt{mask\_sanitized}}(a_{b}), (13)
SbL\displaystyle S_{b}^{L} =p^borig​(ab)−p^borig_sanitized​(ab).\displaystyle=\widehat{p}_{b}^{\texttt{orig}}(a_{b})-\widehat{p}_{b}^{\texttt{orig\_sanitized}}(a_{b}). (14)

SbUS_{b}^{U} is the observed-mediator user-view substitution score, indicating whether the pending proposal is no longer reproduced once the observed user view is replaced by the masking probe, and SbMS_{b}^{M} is the probe-conditional mediator-purification score, indicating whether the selected spans account for the probe-induced action. SbRS_{b}^{R} is its sanitized-mediator counterpart, indicating whether the same proposal remains user-anchored once the implicated content is removed, while SbLS_{b}^{L} is the user-preserving mediator-purification score: both of its regimes retain the observed user view, so it indicates whether the pending proposal survives that removal under the user’s own request. The takeover decision uses SbLS_{b}^{L} and SbMS_{b}^{M} at the current boundary and the trends of SbUS_{b}^{U} and SbMS_{b}^{M} across the window, with SbRS_{b}^{R} retained for trace-level analysis; whether a purified continuation is admitted is determined in Stage 2.

IV-F Stage 1: Takeover Detection

A boundary is applicable to the local replay test when the original proposal is nonempty, a control-positive probe-induced action is available so that SbMS_{b}^{M} is defined, and the required sanitized comparisons are executable. At all other boundaries we set SbU=SbM=SbL=0S_{b}^{U}=S_{b}^{M}=S_{b}^{L}=0 and Lb=0L_{b}=0 as a zero-fill convention.

Boundary-local attribution. At an applicable boundary, AgentSentry defines

Lb=𝕀[SbL>δL∧SbM>δM].L_{b}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[S_{b}^{L}>\delta_{L}\land S_{b}^{M}>\delta_{M}\right]. (15)

The gate requires both user-preserving mediator sensitivity of the pending proposal and corroborating probe evidence; the masked comparison alone cannot establish takeover.

Temporal aggregation. The local gate is referenced to the pending proposal and therefore remains silent while mediator influence is present but not yet acted upon. To capture a progressive shift from user-supported to mediator-supported behavior, AgentSentry retains the attribution scores over the sliding window Wb={max⁡(1,b−w+1),…,b}W_{b}=\{\max(1,b-w+1),\ldots,b\} and forms the histories

𝐬bU=(SuU)u∈Wb,𝐬bM=(SuM)u∈Wb.\mathbf{s}_{b}^{U}=\bigl(S_{u}^{U}\bigr)_{u\in W_{b}},\qquad\mathbf{s}_{b}^{M}=\bigl(S_{u}^{M}\bigr)_{u\in W_{b}}. (16)

Ordinary least-squares fitting yields

βbU=slope⁡(𝐬bU),βbM=slope⁡(𝐬bM),\beta_{b}^{U}=\operatorname{slope}(\mathbf{s}_{b}^{U}),\qquad\beta_{b}^{M}=\operatorname{slope}(\mathbf{s}_{b}^{M}), (17)

evaluated only when |Wb|=w|W_{b}|=w; before a complete window is available we set βbU=βbM=0\beta_{b}^{U}=\beta_{b}^{M}=0. A negative βbU\beta_{b}^{U} indicates weakening user-view anchoring, whereas a positive βbM\beta_{b}^{M} indicates increasing probe-conditional mediator dependence. The temporal replay risk is

ℛb=12​([−βbU]++[βbM]+),[v]+≜max⁡{v,0}.\mathcal{R}_{b}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\left[-\beta_{b}^{U}\right]_{+}+\left[\beta_{b}^{M}\right]_{+}\right),\qquad[v]_{+}\triangleq\max\{v,0\}. (18)

Because a declining user-view score alone does not establish mediator control, the temporal branch additionally requires HbM=𝕀[maxu∈WbSuM>δM]H_{b}^{M}=\mathbb{I}[\max_{u\in W_{b}}S_{u}^{M}>\delta_{M}].

Delayed action realization. Let MbM_{b} denote the delayed-match indicator defined in Appendix B, which records whether the current pending action structurally matches a recent control-positive, purification-sensitive, and consequential probe-induced action. The replay-attributed takeover indicator is

𝖳𝖺𝗄𝖾𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋b=𝕀[Lb=1∨(ℛb≥γ∧HbM=1)∨Mb=1].\mathsf{Takeover}_{b}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[L_{b}=1\lor\left(\mathcal{R}_{b}\geq\gamma\land H_{b}^{M}=1\right)\lor M_{b}=1\right]. (19)

The first clause captures an abrupt boundary-local takeover, the second a progressive user-to-mediator shift across recent boundaries, even where no single boundary satisfies the local gate, and the third delayed realization of a previously attributed control action.

The reported configuration uses w=3w=3 and a configured replay budget K=1K=1, with deterministic replays collapsed to one effective outcome per regime. The decision parameters are

(δL,δM,γ)=(0, 0, 0.25).(\delta_{L},\delta_{M},\gamma)=\left(0,\,0,\,0.25\right). (20)

Here δL\delta_{L} and δM\delta_{M} are the minimum positive attribution contrasts and γ\gamma is the temporal alarm threshold; with binary scores over a three-boundary window, γ=0.25\gamma=0.25 is attained by a maximal change in either trend. With zero-filled inapplicable boundaries, this clause also fires at the first post-warm-up boundary with SbM>δMS_{b}^{M}>\delta_{M}, even if SbL=0S_{b}^{L}=0 (Appendix D). Window warm-up and sensitivity are described in Appendix A-C.

IV-G Stage 2: Boundary Repair and Safe Continuation

When 𝖳𝖺𝗄𝖾𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋b=0\mathsf{Takeover}_{b}=0, AgentSentry preserves the boundary state and the pending proposal. When 𝖳𝖺𝗄𝖾𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋b=1\mathsf{Takeover}_{b}=1, it repairs the implicated mediator view and re-derives the pending continuation under the sanitized state. Reusing the sanitized mediator constructed during attribution diagnosis, AgentSentry forms

cb(san)=hb⊕xb⊕rb(san)c_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})}=h_{b}\oplus x_{b}\oplus r_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})} (21)

and derives the revised proposal

a~b=𝖱𝖾𝗏𝗂𝗌𝖾⁡(ab(san),g,Π,cb(san)).\widetilde{a}_{b}=\mathsf{Revise}\left(a_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})};g,\Pi,c_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})}\right). (22)

𝖱𝖾𝗏𝗂𝗌𝖾\mathsf{Revise} reuses ab(san)a_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})} when it provides a non-redundant, user-supported continuation; otherwise it invokes the same agent backbone from cb(san)c_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})} to obtain a continuation consistent with the trusted goal and deployment policy. A proposed effect is admitted only when its endpoint is permitted under that policy and each policy-sensitive argument it carries is supported by the trusted request, the trusted runtime state, or the retained purified evidence; when no such continuation exists, 𝖱𝖾𝗏𝗂𝗌𝖾\mathsf{Revise} returns a non-effectful response. The boundary-local continuation rule is

(cb(safe),ab(safe))={(cb,ab),𝖳𝖺𝗄𝖾𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋b=0,(cb(san),a~b),𝖳𝖺𝗄𝖾𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋b=1.(c_{b}^{(\mathrm{safe})},a_{b}^{(\mathrm{safe})})=\begin{cases}(c_{b},a_{b}),&\mathsf{Takeover}_{b}=0,\\[3.0pt] (c_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})},\widetilde{a}_{b}),&\mathsf{Takeover}_{b}=1.\end{cases} (23)

This repair is deliberately local. AgentSentry neither rolls back the trajectory nor disables tool use: it removes the attributed mediator control, re-derives the continuation under the repaired boundary state, and resumes the original workflow whenever a supported continuation remains. Algorithm 1 summarizes the per-boundary procedure.

V Evaluation

We evaluate AgentSentry primarily on the AgentDojo benchmark [10], which provides controlled multi-hop tool execution, structured external feedback, and adversarial context perturbations. Unlike evaluations that examine single-turn prompt manipulations [31, 28], we focus on settings where external signals accumulate across turns and influence tool selection in later stages. We further report an OpenClaw engineering case study [23, 24] covering calendar, drive, email, filesystem, and web workflows in a deployed-style local-agent setting.

V-A Experimental Setup

Model Selection. We evaluate three black-box backbones spanning different capability levels and design ecosystems: GPT-4o, a high-capability model widely adopted in recent agent benchmarks [10]; GPT-3.5-turbo, a less capable but widely deployed model; and Qwen3-Max, a strong model from an alternative training and alignment ecosystem. All are accessed strictly as black boxes and receive identical system prompts, tool interfaces, and environments.

Datasets and Tasks. All experiments use the four standard AgentDojo suites, Travel, Workspace, Banking, and Slack [10], which cover itinerary construction, document and file manipulation, constrained transactional workflows, and multi-party communication. Each instance induces a sequence of tool invocations that combine intermediate outputs with evolving conversational context, so external content can influence later decisions. We adopt the latest public release (v0.1.35), in which the Workspace suite expands from 66 to 1414 injection tasks and the total number of security test cases increases from 629629 to 949949. AgentDojo records turn-level traces of model messages, tool calls and arguments, return values, and state transitions, which supply the mediator variables required for controlled re-execution.

Attack Types. We evaluate three IPI families that manipulate contextual signals returned by external tools. Important Instructions [10] injects authority- or urgency-marked directives into free-text tool returns, framed as mandatory preliminary steps. Tool Knowledge [10] embeds documentation-style guidance, including tool names and argument specifications, biasing the agent toward a particular invocation or parameter choice. InjecAgent [28] inserts concise imperative overrides into structured metadata fields ordinarily treated as factual records.

OpenClaw engineering case study. Beyond AgentDojo, we conduct a surface-balanced case study on OpenClaw, a representative local-agent platform for end-to-end security evaluation [23, 24]. It is not a second aggregate benchmark; it documents the implementation and selectivity of AgentSentry’s boundary instrumentation. Across five surfaces, we instantiate attacked workflows with weak and strong injected artifacts together with matched benign workflows over the same tools, and report takeover and benign alarms in Section V-G.

Defense Mechanisms. We use No Defense as the undefended reference and compare AgentSentry against representative inference-time defenses in five categories, all evaluated under identical task suites, attack configurations, tool interfaces, and backbone settings. Model-based detection is represented by a DeBERTa-v3 classifier applied to tool-returned content [44]. Prompt-level augmentation includes Delimiting [45], which marks external content with explicit textual boundaries, and Repeat Prompt [54], which restates the user objective around the incorporated context. Tool-policy and dependency constraints include Tool Filter [10], an invocation allowlist, and IPIGuard [48], which constrains execution through a tool-dependency graph. Agent-level and runtime-trace guards include MELON and MELON-Aug [16], based on masked trajectory re-execution; Task Shield [17], which blocks steps misaligned with the user objective; AgentArmor [49], which applies program analysis to runtime traces; and TraceAegis [50], which combines hierarchical trace analysis with anomaly detection. Attribution- and provenance-based defenses include CausalArmor [51], which ablates and sanitizes untrusted context segments; AttriGuard [52], which attributes each proposed invocation independently under a control-attenuated view of external observations; and ProvSEEK [53], which performs LLM-driven provenance forensics.

Collectively, these baselines form a representative comparison set for assessing AgentSentry’s security–utility trade-off.

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate security and task performance using four metrics summarized in Table I: Attack Success Rate (ASR, ↓\downarrow), Utility Under Attack (UA, ↑\uparrow), Clean Utility (CU, ↑\uparrow), and False Positive Rate (FPR, ↓\downarrow). In addition, to characterize AgentSentry’s deployment cost, we measure attacked- and benign-path end-to-end latency, total model calls, and token consumption on benchmark-scale AgentDojo workflows.

Research Questions. We evaluate AgentSentry by addressing:

  • •

    RQ1: How effective is AgentSentry at mitigating multi-turn IPI across attack families and black-box LLM backbones, as quantified by the ASR–UA trade-off?

  • •

    RQ2: Which attribution components are necessary to attain the observed security–utility frontier (ablation)?

  • •

    RQ3: Are takeover alarms mechanistically interpretable and temporally well-localized at tool-return boundaries?

  • •

    RQ4: Does AgentSentry remain effective under delayed, memory-propagated, and distributed injections, and under adaptive attacks?

  • •

    RQ5: What latency, call, and token cost does AgentSentry incur on attacked and benign executions?

We additionally report an OpenClaw engineering case study, which uses a distinct local-agent harness and reports workflow-level alarm counts rather than benchmark-defined task utility.

V-B Security–Utility Frontier Across Attack Families and Backbones (RQ1)

Table II reports security and utility across the four AgentDojo suites, stratified by attack family and backbone, and Figure 3 plots the corresponding operating points using ASR and UA averaged over the three attack families, with the upper-left region indicating lower attack success and higher task completion. Results for AgentArmor, TraceAegis, and ProvSEEK appear in Appendix C.

Baseline vulnerability: tool-mediated context creates a persistent control channel. The undefended agent remains vulnerable across all three backbones, with average ASR of 26.17%26.17\%, 38.93%38.93\%, and 33.22%33.22\%. The largest single failure is Tool Knowledge on GPT-3.5-turbo, where ASR reaches 73.57%73.57\% and UA drops to 16.43%16.43\%. Qwen3-Max attains the strongest benign performance (CU 85.57%85.57\%) yet still records 60.71%60.71\% ASR under the same family, indicating that the attack surface follows from long-context tool-augmented execution rather than from weaker backbones.

Prompt-only mitigation leaves substantial residual attack success. Prompt-level defenses improve UA in some settings but do not separate trusted user goals from untrusted tool-mediated content. Repeat Prompt raises UA under Important Instructions to 61.35%61.35\% on GPT-4o and 65.41%65.41\% on Qwen3-Max, yet average ASR remains 18.61%18.61\% and 29.81%29.81\%. These results suggest that reinforcing the user instruction is insufficient once attacker-written directives are embedded in tool outputs that appear task-relevant.

Filtering, dependency, and content-based defenses reduce ASR through conservative control, but yield brittle availability. Tool Filter reduces average ASR to 5.58%5.58\% and 6.99%6.99\% on GPT-4o and GPT-3.5-turbo, but this operating point does not transfer: on Qwen3-Max it records zero successful attacks while CU falls to 6.19%6.19\% and FPR rises to 95.88%95.88\%, consistent with rigid allowlisting truncating legitimate multi-step workflows. The DeBERTa detector shows a related limitation, with benign FPR between 60.82%60.82\% and 64.95%64.95\% and average UA between 17.83%17.83\% and 30.20%30.20\%, suggesting that surface-form classification removes task-relevant evidence without isolating instruction-bearing influence. IPIGuard attains the highest baseline UA under Tool Knowledge on all three backbones (66.43%66.43\%, 67.86%67.86\%, 69.29%69.29\%), but its ASR under the same family remains 5.71%5.71\%, 14.29%14.29\%, and 16.43%16.43\% with benign FPR near 40%40\%, consistent with dependency constraints preserving valid tool-use paths while remaining vulnerable to malicious guidance embedded in a plausible execution path.

Trajectory- and alignment-level guards reduce ASR but sacrifice task completion under ambiguous context. MELON, MELON-Aug, and Task Shield reduce ASR under Important Instructions and InjecAgent, but degrade under Tool Knowledge, where injected content appears as plausible procedural guidance rather than an overt override. On GPT-4o, MELON records zero successful attacks under Important Instructions at only 18.05%18.05\% UA, and MELON-Aug attains 37.14%37.14\% UA under Tool Knowledge; Task Shield behaves similarly. These outcomes are consistent with detection-first semantics that resolve ambiguity by rejecting the action or truncating the workflow.

Attribution-oriented defenses improve utility but remain limited by coverage and intervention selectivity. CausalArmor [51] records average ASR of 12.23%12.23\%, 12.95%12.95\%, and 12.02%12.02\% across GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo, and Qwen3-Max, respectively. Its benign FPR ranges from 45.36%45.36\% to 65.98%65.98\%, while its average UA remains between 48.07%48.07\% and 55.92%55.92\%. This result reflects the difficulty of using attribution-guided sanitization to remove control-bearing content without discarding task-relevant evidence. Insufficient intervention can leave residual attacker influence, whereas broader intervention can suppress legitimate context and reduce both benign and attacked-task utility. AttriGuard [52] provides the strongest evaluated baseline in terms of average UA, attaining 72.29%72.29\%, 67.68%67.68\%, and 74.89%74.89\% across the three backbones. Its action-level attribution therefore preserves substantially more utility than earlier trajectory- and alignment-level guards. Nevertheless, its average ASR remains 4.15%4.15\%, 1.54%1.54\%, and 7.26%7.26\%, while its benign FPR remains 25.77%25.77\%, 20.62%20.62\%, and 23.71%23.71\%, respectively. Action-level attribution is less discriminative when benign and attack-induced continuations yield similar proposed invocations, which can leave residual malicious influence. Conversely, modifying external evidence during attribution can alter benign actions that legitimately depend on that evidence, leading to unnecessary intervention.

AgentSentry attains the most favorable observed aggregate security–utility operating point. Across all nine attack-family/backbone combinations, AgentSentry is the only evaluated defense to record zero observed successful attacks in every combination. It also achieves the highest average UA on all three backbones: 74.13%74.13\% on GPT-4o, 71.69%71.69\% on GPT-3.5-turbo, and 82.49%82.49\% on Qwen3-Max. Its benign CU is 76.29%76.29\%, 75.26%75.26\%, and 80.41%80.41\%, with FPR of 2.06%2.06\%, 5.15%5.15\%, and 4.12%4.12\%, respectively. These results place AgentSentry in the most favorable observed operating region in Figure 3.

Comparison with the strongest evaluated baseline. Compared with the strongest baseline by average UA, AgentSentry improves average UA by 1.841.84, 4.014.01, and 7.607.60 percentage points on GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo, and Qwen3-Max, respectively. At the same time, it reduces the baseline’s residual average ASR of 4.15%4.15\%, 1.54%1.54\%, and 7.26%7.26\% to zero observed successful attacks. AgentSentry also lowers benign FPR from 25.77%25.77\%, 20.62%20.62\%, and 23.71%23.71\% to 2.06%2.06\%, 5.15%5.15\%, and 4.12%4.12\%, respectively. Thus, the improvement reflects both higher attacked-task utility and greater benign selectivity, rather than an ASR reduction obtained through more aggressive blocking.

Why temporal attribution diagnostics improve the trade-off. The comparison shows that the security–utility trade-off depends not only on whether a defense performs attribution, but also on the unit of diagnosis and how the resulting evidence is translated into mitigation. Prompt- and content-level defenses filter external evidence, whereas tool-policy, dependency-, and trajectory-level defenses constrain the actions that may follow. These interventions can suppress attacks, but may also remove task-relevant evidence or truncate legitimate multi-step execution. Attribution-oriented defenses localize suspicious influence more directly and therefore preserve greater utility. CausalArmor attributes influence to untrusted context segments, whereas AttriGuard attributes individual proposed tool invocations. However, identifying an influential segment or invocation does not by itself ensure that the implicated influence can be removed while preserving a valid continuation of the original task. This distinction is reflected in their remaining ASR and FPR in Table II. AgentSentry performs attribution diagnosis at the tool-return boundary where untrusted mediator content enters the execution state. Its controlled contrasts assess both whether the pending behavior is sensitive to the unsanitized mediator and whether task-consistent continuation remains recoverable after purification. AgentSentry then applies the same localized mediator transformation during mitigation and re-derives the pending action under the sanitized state. This alignment of diagnosis, localized repair, and continued execution preserves task-relevant evidence while suppressing the control-bearing influence associated with the pending deviation. The observed combination of zero successful attacks, high average UA, and low benign FPR is consistent with the selectivity of this diagnose-and-continue design. Appendix D gives a representative example, including its boundary-local attribution outcome and purified continuation.

Finite-sample uncertainty. Zero observed attacks do not establish a zero population attack rate. For each backbone, AgentSentry records 0/9490/949 successful attacks; the two-sided exact Clopper–Pearson 95%95\% confidence interval is [0.00%,0.39%][0.00\%,0.39\%]. On the 9797 benign tasks per backbone, AgentSentry records 2/97=2.06%2/97=2.06\% interventions for GPT-4o (95%95\% CI: [0.25%,7.25%][0.25\%,7.25\%]), 5/97=5.15%5/97=5.15\% for GPT-3.5-turbo ([1.69%,11.62%][1.69\%,11.62\%]), and 4/97=4.12%4/97=4.12\% for Qwen3-Max ([1.13%,10.22%][1.13\%,10.22\%]). These intervals quantify finite-sample binomial uncertainty; they do not capture model-version drift, provider-side changes, or run-to-run API variation.

The AgentDojo traces are predominantly short-horizon. We therefore construct a dedicated stress suite spanning delayed triggers, persistent-memory poisoning, and distributed accumulation over artifact horizons L∈{3,6,12,24}L\in\{3,6,12,24\}.

V-C Component Ablations (RQ2)

We conduct a targeted ablation study to identify which design choices in AgentSentry are necessary to sustain a strong security–utility trade-off, and which components contribute only incremental gains. Each variant relaxes exactly one component while holding the remaining pipeline fixed, and all are evaluated on Workspace (560 tasks) under the Important Instructions attack family with Qwen3-Max.

Ablation dimensions. Table III reports variants that relax distinct stages of the diagnose-and-continue pipeline. Mediator purification disabled sets rb(san)=rbr_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})}=r_{b}, so the sanitized regimes reuse the observed mediator and the replay contrasts no longer test whether a pending proposal persists once instruction-carrying content is neutralized. To assess intervention design, the two Weak masking variants replace the structured probe xmaskx^{\mathrm{mask}} with lighter perturbations (paraphrasing or tool-instruction deletion), preserving the controlled re-execution protocol but weakening the intended separation between user-supported and mediator-sensitive behavior. We then ablate the takeover decision logic by removing immediate boundary-local attribution (Boundary-local gate disabled), windowed trend aggregation (Temporal aggregation disabled), or recognition of a previously attributed objective when its action later becomes live (Delayed matching disabled). Finally, Block-only intervention retains the complete attribution diagnosis and takeover decision but terminates the workflow at an alarm, isolating the contribution of purified continuation from that of detection.

Ablation analysis. Table III shows that the observed security–utility profile is dominated by mediator-side purification and the fidelity of the masking intervention, rather than by the auxiliary decision branches. The full system attains UA=92.32\mathrm{UA}=92.32 with ASR=0.00\mathrm{ASR}=0.00. Disabling mediator purification causes a sharp degradation to UA=58.21\mathrm{UA}=58.21 and ASR=22.50\mathrm{ASR}=22.50, returning the pipeline to approximately the undefended operating point: once the sanitized and observed mediators coincide, no replay contrast can distinguish a mediator-dependent proposal and all three takeover branches remain inactive. Both Weak masking variants yield comparably unfavorable trade-offs (UA=58.93\mathrm{UA}=58.93 with ASR=21.07\mathrm{ASR}=21.07 under paraphrasing, and UA=60.36\mathrm{UA}=60.36 with ASR=19.82\mathrm{ASR}=19.82 under tool-instruction deletion), suggesting that lightweight perturbations identify control-bearing content less reliably, so fewer boundaries admit a non-identity purification. Among the decision branches, removing the boundary-local gate is by far the most damaging (UA=60.71\mathrm{UA}=60.71, ASR=19.64\mathrm{ASR}=19.64), since injected objectives in this suite commonly become purification-sensitive at the same boundary at which the pending proposal first deviates. Temporal aggregation and delayed matching retain relatively high utility (UA=89.82\mathrm{UA}=89.82 and 91.4391.43) but incur non-zero ASR=1.96\mathrm{ASR}=1.96 and 1.071.07, respectively. Finally, Block-only intervention preserves zero observed attack success but falls to UA=55.36\mathrm{UA}=55.36, below the undefended reference, isolating the 207207 workflows that are completed only through purified continuation.

Takeaway. Overall, the ablation results support that AgentSentry’s effectiveness is fundamentally grounded in mediator-side purification enabled by the structured masking probe, and in the boundary-local attribution it makes available. Auxiliary branches such as temporal aggregation and delayed matching improve coverage in specific settings, but removing mediator purification or weakening the probe leads to a pronounced collapse in both security and utility. Purified continuation contributes no additional attack suppression, yet accounts for the entire utility separation from a detect-and-terminate pipeline at the same operating point.

V-D Attribution Alignment and Takeover Localization (RQ3)

To examine how the takeover decision aligns with boundary-local replay evidence, we trace the attribution scores of Section IV-F across the tool-return boundaries of a representative Workspace instance (u20-i6) under the Important Instructions attack family. The payload is absent from the user request and is instead embedded in the description field returned by get_day_calendar_events, directing the agent to read the user’s unread email, forward its contents to an attacker-controlled recipient, and delete the sent message before resuming the scheduling task.

Figure 4 reports the four score sequences, SbU=[1,1,1]S_{b}^{U}=[1,1,1], SbM=[1,1,1]S_{b}^{M}=[1,1,1], SbR=[1,1,0]S_{b}^{R}=[1,1,0], and SbL=[0,0,1]S_{b}^{L}=[0,0,1]. At b=1b=1 and b=2b=2, the masking probe already exposes the injected email objective, and the probe-induced action does not survive mask_sanitized, yielding SbM=1S_{b}^{M}=1. The pending live proposals, however, are the user-supported contact lookup and calendar-event creation. Both retain their structural signature under orig_sanitized, so SbL=0S_{b}^{L}=0 and the local gate remains closed; as the window is still warming up, no alarm is raised. The positive SbRS_{b}^{R} further indicates that these benign proposals remain anchored by the user request after purification. At b=3b=3, the live replay proposes get_unread_emails. This action does not survive orig_sanitized, yielding S3L=1S_{3}^{L}=1, and the probe-induced action again disappears under mask_sanitized, yielding S3M=1S_{3}^{M}=1; since the proposal survives neither sanitized regime, S3R=0S_{3}^{R}=0. Figure 5 shows the resulting decision quantities. With (δL,δM)=(0,0)(\delta_{L},\delta_{M})=(0,0) the boundary-local gate gives L3=1L_{3}=1. Over the same window β3U=β3M=0\beta_{3}^{U}=\beta_{3}^{M}=0, so ℛ3=0<γ\mathcal{R}_{3}=0<\gamma and the temporal branch is not exercised: the first alarm b⋆=3b^{\star}=3 is attributable to the boundary-local gate alone. The pending email-read action is withheld, AgentSentry continues from the sanitized mediator state, and the execution completes the requested lunch event without reading, forwarding, or deleting email.

Takeover timing across the benchmark. Aggregating takeover timing over all attack instances in AgentDojo, injected instructions in most runs become actionable immediately after a contaminated tool return is incorporated into the boundary state, so the malicious span can bias the next-step proposal without additional dialogue turns; AgentSentry accordingly localizes takeover at, or immediately after, the first affected tool read. A smaller subset exhibits delayed actionability, in which the injected span propagates through later reasoning or commitment behavior and the alarm follows within one to two turns, only rarely at the final response.

V-E Long-Horizon Scalability and Targeted Robustness (RQ4)

The standard AgentDojo evaluation is dominated by short attack horizons and by attack constructions that are not tailored to the defense. We therefore conduct three complementary stress evaluations with separate protocols and denominators.

Long-horizon injection. The suite crosses two dimensions: the propagation family, being delayed trigger, persistent-memory poisoning, or distributed accumulation, and the attack surface, being argument-level recipient manipulation or scope-level silent over-collection. Each family is evaluated at L∈{3,6,12,24}L\in\{3,6,12,24\} with four workflows per surface in every cell, giving 96 attacked workflows and 96 matched benign controls. AgentSentry prevents 85 of the 96 injected objectives, an ASR of 11.46%11.46\% and a UA of 88.54%88.54\%, and intervenes on 9 of 96 benign controls. Protection is strongest at short horizons and degrades as source evidence must survive longer intervals, memory transitions, and multi-source composition. Among baselines with non-zero utility, CausalArmor is the strongest at 37 successful attacks and AttriGuard reaches 71; MELON records 32 only by withholding the requested send, and thus zero strict utility.

The two surfaces exercise different parts of the decision rule. Argument-level manipulation typically changes the complete endpoint–argument signature at the final effectful boundary, so the user-preserving boundary-local contrast supplies most of the protection on this evaluated surface. Scope-level over-collection preserves the authorized send endpoint and recipient while altering the provenance of the message body through earlier out-of-scope reads, and the deviation appears only as a trend across adjacent boundaries. Disabling temporal aggregation accordingly raises scope-level ASR from 7/48 to 43/48, close to the undefended rate, while changing argument-level ASR by a single workflow. The temporal clause is thus redundant where a boundary-local contrast already exposes the deviation, and load-bearing where it does not.

Mechanism-targeted adaptive attacks. The adaptive study holds workflow length fixed and instead varies the attack construction against the replay, purification, provenance, and commitment mechanisms, since adaptive attacks are known to break IPI defenses [55]. Of 36 transformations, 19 activate in their same-case undefended controls. AgentSentry prevents 17 of these, raises an alarm in 18, and localizes 17 within one boundary. Every activated trigger-position, cross-return, and probe-aware transformation is blocked; both survivors are factual-recipient-poisoning cases, in which the mediator supplies an effect-bearing argument as plausible metadata rather than as instruction-bearing control. Replay tests dependence on grounded control spans but does not adjudicate the truth of a plausible field value, which delimits the scope of instruction-oriented purification. Appendix E details each transformation.

Operator and threshold sensitivity. We further vary the configuration choices the defense itself controls. Applying purification at every boundary for which the masking probe produces a control-positive audit record reaches comparable attack survival but intervenes on 21 of 36 benign controls against 6 of 36 under the deployed configuration: attribution does not strengthen purification; it makes purification selective. Projection width matters independently, since halving each grounded span raises attack survival from 2/19 to 6/19 while leaving benign intervention unchanged. Stripping the enclosing markup from the injected artifacts leaves conditional attack survival essentially unchanged, at two of 17 activated cases against two of 19, so the operator is keyed to grounded control spans rather than to a fixed delimiter. Raising (δL,δM,γ)(\delta_{L},\delta_{M},\gamma) raises attack survival from 2/19 to 5/19 as the temporal clause is disabled, and crossing the attribution boundary suppresses intervention entirely. Four practical limits of the deployed configuration remain: residual attacker state outside the sanitized mediator view, projection of procedural evidence a benign task depends on, factual parameter poisoning, and over-sanitization when malicious and task-supporting content share a span.

V-F Runtime and Resource Overhead (RQ5)

We evaluate benchmark-scale overhead with Qwen3-Max on all 560560 Workspace/Important Instructions attack executions and all 9797 benign AgentDojo tasks retained by the resource-logging pipeline. We report mean end-to-end (E2E) latency, total model calls, and token consumption separately for attacked and benign executions. E2E latency covers the realized execution from the user request to the final response, whereas total calls and tokens include both committed live execution and defense-side model invocations.

Attacked executions. Relative to No Defense, AgentSentry increases mean E2E latency from 26.3726.37 to 50.1050.10 seconds (1.90×1.90\times), total model calls from 4.534.53 to 9.599.59 (2.12×2.12\times), and token consumption from 13,79713{,}797 to 27,48027{,}480 (1.99×1.99\times). These totals reflect both controlled replay and the realized live trajectory: suppressing an injected branch can shorten committed execution even while the defense performs additional diagnostic work.

Benign executions. On benign workflows, AgentSentry increases mean E2E latency from 17.0917.09 to 37.9537.95 seconds (2.22×2.22\times), total model calls from 4.494.49 to 8.048.04 (1.79×1.79\times), and token consumption from 4,6544{,}654 to 11,69811{,}698 (2.51×2.51\times). Benign executions contain no attack-induced branch whose removal can offset diagnostic work, yet they still incur boundary-local attribution diagnosis before the runtime can determine that no repair is required.

Comparison with other defenses. The overhead of AgentSentry is of the same order as that of other defenses that perform execution-time analysis. On attacked executions, its mean E2E latency (50.10 s) is lower than that of AttriGuard (53.17 s), ProvSEEK (54.40 s), AgentArmor (55.94 s), and TraceAegis (83.80 s), and it issues fewer model calls per case (9.59) than AgentArmor (11.66), TraceAegis (16.35), and ProvSEEK (16.62), although more than AttriGuard (7.91). Prompt-level and filter-based defenses cost less but operate at a less favorable security–utility point (Table II).

Cost interpretation. The four controlled re-execution regimes specify the logical attribution protocol rather than four additional model calls at every boundary. The runtime may reuse the live orig proposal, reuse unsanitized outcomes when mediator purification is the identity, and invoke revision or commitment checks only when required. Controlled replay accounts for most of the added latency, whereas deterministic mediator purification requires no separate purification-model invocation.

V-G OpenClaw Engineering Case Study

We further evaluate AgentSentry in a surface-balanced OpenClaw engineering case study in a deployed-style local agent setting. The study covers five workspace surfaces: calendar, drive, email, filesystem, and web. It reports workflow-level takeover alarms on attack workflows and matched benign controls. AgentSentry raises takeover alarms in 113 of 120 attack workflows and in 2 of 60 matched benign controls. Both benign alarms occur on the Web surface. Among the seven attack workflows without a takeover alarm, four yield no aligned evidence span during probing, two reach the takeover decision stage but remain below the configured decision criterion, and one exhibits run-level output variation.

VI Conclusion

We propose AgentSentry, an application-layer inference-time defense against indirect prompt injection in tool-augmented LLM agents. AgentSentry performs boundary-local counterfactual replay at tool-return boundaries to determine whether a pending structural proposal is sensitive to grounded mediator content. When the takeover rule is satisfied, it purifies the implicated content and resumes execution under a sanitized state rather than terminating the workflow. On AgentDojo, across four task suites, three IPI families, and three black-box LLM backbones, AgentSentry records zero observed successful attacks and achieves an average UA of 76.10%76.10\%, improving UA by 1.841.84 to 7.607.60 percentage points over the strongest evaluated baseline while reducing its residual average ASR of 1.54%1.54\% to 7.26%7.26\% to zero observed successes. Dedicated stress suites delimit this result: ASR is 11.46%11.46\% on long-horizon workflows, where protection depends on source evidence remaining groundable across extended injection-to-effect intervals, and conditional attack survival is 10.53%10.53\% under mechanism-targeted adaptive attacks, where the residual cases are confined to factual parameter poisoning. An OpenClaw engineering case study additionally documents the trace-level behavior of the boundary instrumentation in a deployed-style local-agent runtime. These results suggest that boundary-local diagnosis with purified continuation is a practical direction for protecting action-capable agents in tool-mediated settings, provided that the originating source remains recoverable when the injected effect becomes actionable.

Ethics Considerations

This work studies defenses against indirect prompt injection in tool-augmented LLM agents. The evaluated attacks are conducted only in controlled benchmark environments and do not target live users, real accounts, or production services. Our goal is to reduce the risk of unauthorized tool use and data exfiltration by enabling runtime diagnosis and mitigation. We avoid releasing executable attack code against real systems or instructions that would enable deployment-specific abuse. The artifacts released with this paper focus on reproducible benchmark evaluation, defense logic, and sanitized examples. The study does not involve human subjects or private user data, and all experiments are performed on public or synthetic benchmark tasks. The OpenClaw case study uses synthetic workspace artifacts and sandboxed tools and does not access live user accounts, production services, or real personal data. We believe these measures mitigate the main dual-use and operational risks associated with this work.

Appendix A Action Matching and Replay Configuration

A-A Action Matching and Representative Proposals

The canonicalization operator ν⁡(⋅)\nu(\cdot) removes serialization-only variation while preserving the complete argument content used for matching. Mappings are traversed under a stable key order; sequence-valued arguments are canonicalized element-wise and sorted by their normalized representation; and scalar values are converted to trimmed, case-folded strings with consecutive whitespace collapsed. Missing arguments remain explicit placeholders and are not inferred from surrounding context.

Before signature construction, the parser normalizes function, name, and tool as endpoint aliases, and args and arguments as argument-map aliases. Endpoint names must satisfy the registered identifier syntax, and an argument payload must be a mapping. Parsing a candidate does not authorize it or permit execution.

Consistent with Eq. (6), tool-bearing proposals are compared as order-insensitive sets of endpoint–argument pairs. Two proposals match only when they contain the same normalized endpoint–argument pairs. For a text-only proposal, equality is defined over ν⁡(nl⁡(a))\nu(\mathrm{nl}(a)); the runtime may store a stable hash of that value as a compact representation. A proposal with neither tool calls nor nonempty text maps to the 𝙽𝙾𝙾𝙿\mathtt{NOOP} signature. For a regime ι\iota with KbK_{b} available outcomes, let

σ¯bι∈arg​maxs∑k=1Kb𝕀[σ(ab(ι,k))=s].\bar{\sigma}_{b}^{\iota}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{s}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{b}}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\sigma\!\left(a_{b}^{(\iota,k)}\right)=s\right]. (24)

Ties are resolved by replay order. The representative proposal is the first proposal whose signature equals σ¯bι\bar{\sigma}_{b}^{\iota}. The pending proposal aba_{b} is the live-equivalent representative under orig, and ab(san)a_{b}^{(\mathrm{san})} is the representative under orig_sanitized.

The masked reference abmaska_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}} is instantiated only when the masking probe is control-positive and yields a well-formed induced candidate. A valid CONTROL_ATTEMPT: YES record may return NO_TOOL_CALL; in that case no probe-induced action reference is instantiated. If abmaska_{b}^{\mathrm{mask}} is unavailable, we set SbM=0S_{b}^{M}=0, and the boundary is inapplicable to the boundary-local gate.

A-B Replay Budget and Decoding Configuration

Let KK be the configured replay budget and Kb≤KK_{b}\leq K the effective number of outcomes retained for each available regime at boundary bb. The reported evaluation uses deterministic decoding and one effective structural outcome per regime:

K=Kb=1.K=K_{b}=1. (25)

A deployment may configure a larger budget under stochastic decoding. Temporal evidence is accumulated across tool-return boundaries rather than across repeated executions of the same boundary.

All regimes at a boundary use the same model version, system prompt, registered tool schema, cached external returns, and decoding configuration. The orig outcome may reuse the live next-action generation. When purification is the identity, the corresponding unsanitized outcomes are reused. When a required sanitized regime cannot be constructed, it is marked unavailable and no synthetic sanitized-regime outcome is generated.

A-C Window Construction and Fixed Decision Parameters

For an ordered sequence (v1,…,vm)(v_{1},\ldots,v_{m}), the OLS slope used in Eq. (17) is

slope⁡(v1,…,vm)=∑j=1m(j−j¯)​(vj−v¯)∑j=1m(j−j¯)2,\operatorname{slope}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{m})=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{m}(j-\bar{j})(v_{j}-\bar{v})}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}(j-\bar{j})^{2}}, (26)

where j¯=(m+1)/2\bar{j}=(m+1)/2 and v¯=m−1​∑j=1mvj\bar{v}=m^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{m}v_{j}. The physical boundary index continues to advance when a local replay test is inapplicable; such a boundary contributes the zero scores specified in Section IV-F. The temporal branch is evaluated only after a complete window of length ww is available.

The reported operating point is

(w,K,δL,δM,γ)=(3,1,0,0,0.25).(w,K,\delta_{L},\delta_{M},\gamma)=(3,1,0,0,0.25). (27)

Because the local gate uses strict inequalities, δL=δM=0\delta_{L}=\delta_{M}=0 still requires positive attribution scores. With one effective outcome, SbU,SbM∈{0,1}S_{b}^{U},S_{b}^{M}\in\{0,1\}. Over a three-boundary window, a favorable OLS slope has maximum magnitude 1/21/2; hence one maximal favorable trend contributes 0.250.25 to ℛb\mathcal{R}_{b}, while two concordant maximal trends yield ℛb=0.50\mathcal{R}_{b}=0.50. The condition HbM=1H_{b}^{M}=1 prevents a declining user-view score from activating the temporal branch without mediator support in the same window.

These values are fixed for the reported evaluation and are applied uniformly across task suites, attack families, and model backbones.

Appendix B Delayed Action Matching

Let ℰconseq​(a,Π)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{conseq}}(a;\Pi) denote the set of externally visible or state-changing effects contained in proposal aa under policy Π\Pi. We define the consequential-action indicator as
